ScreenR

Find the genes that matter in pooled shRNA screens — with p-values you can trust, quality control built in and publication-ready plots.

ScreenR takes the barcode counts of a pooled shRNA screen and tells you which genes are depleted or enriched by your treatment, how confident you can be in each of them, and whether the result holds up at the level of the single barcodes. It is built on the statistics of edgeR and limma, stores the data in a Bioconductor SummarizedExperiment, and draws every plot with ggplot2.

Why ScreenR?

  • Every hit comes with a p-value and a false discovery rate. The gene-level tests are calibrated: in screens without any real effect about 5% of the genes have p < 0.05, as they should.
  • Benchmarked against the main tools. On simulated screens and on published shRNA (K562) and CRISPR-Cas9 (HAP1) essentiality screens, ScreenR ranks the true hits as well as the best of MAGeCK, BAGEL2, gscreend and plain edgeR/limma workflows, keeps the FDR below the nominal level and runs in seconds (benchmark).
  • Several complementary methods, one table. A permutation test on the barcode Z-scores, limma CAMERA, ROAST and FRY, and an edgeR model for time courses; summarise_hits() combines them and plot_common_hit() shows how they agree.
  • Uses your replicates. Barcode statistics come from the edgeR quasi-likelihood model, so replicate variability is part of the test.
  • Quality control included. Mapped reads, library evenness (Gini index), lost barcodes, replicate correlation and MDS plots, before you look at a single hit.
  • Works with your files as they are. Any column names, sample descriptions from a table, helpful messages when something does not match.
  • shRNA and CRISPR. Works with shRNA and CRISPR-Cas9 libraries, checks the screen with essential and non-essential reference genes (compute_screen_quality()), and corrects CRISPR copy-number bias through CRISPRcleanR (correct_crispr_bias()).
  • Bioconductor native. The ScreenR object is a SummarizedExperiment, so it works with the rest of the Bioconductor ecosystem.

Installation

ScreenR requires R 4.3 or later. Install the release version from Bioconductor:

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages("BiocManager")
}
BiocManager::install("ScreenR")

or the development version from GitHub:

BiocManager::install("EmanuelSoda/ScreenR")

Quick start

The package includes an example screen: shRNA counts for treated (TRT) and control (CTRL) cells at several time points, with three replicates.

library(ScreenR)

data(count_table)
data(annotation_table)
counts <- count_table[count_table$Barcode != "*", ]
colnames(counts) <- c(
    "Barcode", "Time1", "Time2", "Time3_TRT_A", "Time3_TRT_B", "Time3_TRT_C",
    "Time3_CTRL_A", "Time3_CTRL_B", "Time3_CTRL_C",
    "Time4_TRT_A", "Time4_TRT_B", "Time4_TRT_C",
    "Time4_CTRL_A", "Time4_CTRL_B", "Time4_CTRL_C"
)
groups <- factor(c(
    "T1/T2", "T1/T2", rep("Time3_TRT", 3), rep("Time3_CTRL", 3),
    rep("Time4_TRT", 3), rep("Time4_CTRL", 3)
))

# 1. Create the object and normalize the counts
object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts, annotation = annotation_table, groups = groups
)
object <- compute_data_table(normalize_data(remove_all_zero_row(object)))
object
#> class: screenr_object 
#> dim: 5317 14 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(2): counts normalized
#> rownames(5317): 10208 10502 ... 13876 13995
#> rowData names(5): Barcode Gene Gene_ID Sequence Library
#> colnames(14): Time1 Time2 ... Time4_CTRL_B Time4_CTRL_C
#> colData names(4): Sample Day Treatment Group
#> data table: 74438 rows, 9 columns

Check the samples before looking for hits: replicates should cluster together.

plot_mds(object) + ggplot2::theme_bw()

Compare treated and control cells at the last time point with two independent tests, and combine them:

# 2. Define the comparison
design <- create_design_matrix(object)
contrast <- create_contrast(design, treatment = "Time4_TRT", control = "Time4_CTRL")

# 3. Gene-level permutation test on replicate-aware barcode statistics
barcode_statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(object, design, contrast)
zscore <- find_gene_zscore_hit(barcode_statistics, fdr = 1, seed = 1)

# 4. limma CAMERA on the barcodes of each gene
camera <- find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast, fdr = 1)

# 5. One table with the FDR of both methods, best supported genes first
#    (the example screen has a weak effect, so we use a lenient FDR of 25%)
hits <- summarise_hits(list(zscore = zscore, camera = camera), fdr = 0.25)
head(hits)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 6
#>   Gene     FDR_zscore FDR_camera NMethods MaxFDR Hit  
#>   <chr>         <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <lgl>
#> 1 Gene_173      0.128     0.0882        2  0.128 TRUE 
#> 2 Gene_422      0.187     0.0882        2  0.187 TRUE 
#> 3 Gene_15       0.233     0.232         2  0.233 TRUE 
#> 4 Gene_296      0.250     0.0882        2  0.250 TRUE 
#> 5 Gene_370      0.280     0.232         1  0.280 FALSE
#> 6 Gene_352      0.280     0.232         1  0.280 FALSE

Look at the barcodes of the top candidate before trusting it:

top_gene <- as.character(hits$Gene[1])
plot_boxplot(object,
    genes = top_gene, group_var = c("TRT", "CTRL"), fill_var = "Treatment"
) +
    ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(CTRL = "#93B5A3", TRT = "#C9836A")) +
    ggplot2::theme_bw() +
    ggplot2::theme(axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

Which method should I use?

Every method looks for depleted genes by default; set direction = "Up" to find enriched genes (for example in a resistance screen).

Question Function Notes
Which genes are depleted or enriched? find_gene_zscore_hit() Permutation test on the barcode scores; robust default. Use statistic = "median" against off-target effects.
Do the barcodes of a gene change more than the others? find_camera_hit() limma CAMERA, competitive test; works with a single control sample.
Do the barcodes of a gene change at all? find_roast_hit() limma ROAST or FRY (method = "fry"), self-contained; needs replicates in both groups.
Does the effect change over time? find_time_hit() edgeR model of the whole time course.
Which genes are supported by several methods? summarise_hits(), plot_common_hit() One table with the FDR of every method.

How ScreenR compares

In the simulations ScreenR ranks the true hits as well as the best tools and keeps the false discovery rate below the nominal level; at a fixed FDR it is more conservative than MAGeCK MLE and BAGEL2, which find more hits but exceed the nominal FDR in some scenarios. On the published K562 shRNA screen included in the package (k562_count_table) the ScreenR Z-score test is comparable to MAGeCK RRA and BAGEL2. The benchmark article has all the details and reruns the ScreenR side of the comparison.
